chapter_theme: The man's joy in union, in which one person holds all five senses, cures the sickness she caused, and rivals heaven and the virtuous householder's meal. Its last verse compares this desire to knowledge, which only reveals how much more there is.
structure_note: Parimelazhagar's headnotes trace a clandestine narrative: first union (1101), a second meeting (1102), the man's friend objecting (1103), meetings arranged by friends (1104-1106), her friend urging marriage and being put off (1107-1109), and elopement (1110).

1101.reading: The man says that all five senses, seeing, hearing, tasting, smelling and touching, find their objects in this one bright-braceleted woman.
1101.nuance: The claim is about concentration. Parimelazhagar's gloss is that pleasures usually taken from different things at different times are here had at once, from one person. He also folds in the erotic techniques named in Sanskrit treatises, which the verse doesn't mention.

1102.reading: The man says the cure for a disease is usually something other than its cause, but this jewelled woman is herself the cure for the sickness she brings.
1102.nuance: Parimelazhagar sharpens பிற: ordinary medicine is opposite in nature to the disease's cause. Love therefore breaks a rule of medicine, not only of common sense.

1103.reading: The man asks whether the world of the lotus-eyed one can be sweeter than sleeping on the soft arms of the one you love.
1103.nuance: The question is left open, and the commentators answer it for him. Parimelazhagar has the man's friend object that one fit for supreme bliss shouldn't sink to this small pleasure, and takes the man's point to be that heaven requires hard austerities which this sleep does not.

positions.position: The world is Vishnu's, reached by ascetics who renounce the senses; he rejects the Indra reading on the ground that lotus-eyed isn't Indra's name.
positions.quote: தாமரைக்கண்ணான் என்பது அவனுக்குப் பெயரன்மையின், அஃது உரையன்மையறிக.

positions.position: The world is Indra's heaven, and the point is that heaven's pleasure is simply this.

1104.reading: The man asks where she found this fire that burns when he moves away and cools when he comes near.
1104.nuance: Parimelazhagar observes a small sleight: the fire is the man's own desire, which he attributes to her because she is what draws it out.

1105.reading: The man says her shoulders, with flowers in her hair, feel like each thing one craves at the moment of craving it.
1105.nuance: The point is freshness across repetition. For Parimelazhagar, they have already met several times and she still binds him as if new. Manakkudavar's text differs: where the verse has hair adorned with flowers, he has hair fallen loose on her shoulders during love, which changes the picture from adornment to its undoing.

1106.reading: The man says that since her touch makes his life put out fresh shoots each time they meet, this girl's shoulders must be made of ambrosia.
1106.nuance: Ambrosia is inferred from an effect, in the manner of a logical argument. உயிர்தளிர்ப்ப also makes his life a plant, withering between meetings, which Manakkudavar pushes further: without her that life would die.

1107.reading: The man says the embrace of this lovely dark-gold woman is like living in your own home and eating your own food after sharing it.
1107.nuance: A pleasure is measured by a virtue. The comparison brings the whole ethic of the householder into the bedroom, as a kind of satisfaction that has nothing to hide or to owe.

positions.position: Her friend has urged marriage, and he declines: this secret union already gives him the reward of the householder's life.
positions.quote: 'இல்லறஞ்செய்தார் எய்தும் துறக்கத்து இன்பம் எனக்கு இப்புணர்ச்சியே தரும்' என வரைவு உடன்படான் கூறியவாறாயிற்று.

positions.position: The woman embraced is already his wife, so the verse describes married pleasure.
positions.quote: தனது அழகிய காதல் மனைவியைத் தழுவுகின்ற இன்பத்துக்கு

1108.reading: The man says an embrace so close that not even a breeze can part it is sweet to two who desire each other.
1108.nuance: Parimelazhagar finds an evasion in the word இருவர், 'two'. The friend has urged the uninterrupted union of marriage, and he answers that this holds for two people, whereas they are not two. Manakkudavar sees only the praise.

positions.position: He agrees in form but declines the marriage she urges, because here there aren't two.
positions.quote: 'ஈண்டு இருவர் இல்லை இன்மையான், இஃது ஒவ்வாது' என்பது கருத்து.

1109.reading: The man names quarrelling, making up and uniting as the rewards of those who have come together in love.
1109.nuance: The verse puts the quarrel inside love's rewards, and first in the list. That is the seed of the book's final chapter.

positions.position: This is a dismissal: quarrels belong to married men who stray to courtesans, and a couple as one as they are wants no such 'reward'.
positions.quote: அப்பயன் இருதலைப் புள்ளிள் ஓருயிராய் உழுவலன்புடைய எமக்கு வேண்டா

positions.position: This is delight: the man has just ended her sulk and united with her, and celebrates the sequence.
positions.quote: ஊடற் குறிப்புத் தோன்ற நின்ற தலைமகளை ஊடல் தீர்த்துப் புணர்ந்த தலைமகன்

1110.reading: The man says that closeness to this red-jewelled woman works like knowledge: each advance shows how much was lacking before.
1110.nuance: Parimelazhagar closes the chapter by noting that the woman feels this joy too, but it shows in her only through signs and never in speech. Nine verses of male voice therefore rest on a convention, and he says so.

links.note: 343 tells the renunciant to destroy the pull of the five senses and give up all desire at once. 1101 celebrates the same five senses meeting their fill in a single person. The Kural gives each its place in different books without reconciling them.

In 1104 he marvels at a fire that burns at a distance and cools up close. In 1159, a voice in separation says ordinary fire can't burn at a distance at all. The same paradox goes from a delighted question to a complaint.
1065 says even thin gruel earned by your own labour is the sweetest food, for the sake of self-respect. 1107 borrows that dignity of one's own table to describe an embrace.

1109 lists the quarrel as love's reward, and the Kural's last verse, 1330, ends the whole work on the same idea. Parimelazhagar's scornful reading of 1109 is hard to square with the fact that 1330 and the final chapters celebrate the sequence.

396 says knowledge wells up in proportion to study, like water in a sand well. 1110 takes the same unlimited knowledge as the measure of desire, except that in love more of it reveals a lack and not a supply.

source_issues: 1105: Manakkudavar's gloss assumes the reading தோட்டாழ் கதுப்பு where the verse has தோட்டார் கதுப்பு.
1107: Parimelazhagar's gloss has அரிமை where the verse has அரிவை, apparently a typo.
